result: PSAM4-GlyR was selectively expressed in D1-MSNs in the ventral striatum using Cre-dependent viral transduction in prodynorphin-Cre mice crossed with Ai9 reporter mice.
evaluation: Claims C20, C90, and C91 establish the methodological approach and validation of selective PSAM4-GlyR expression. The confocal imaging data in Figure 1A demonstrates colocalization of eGFP (PSAM4-GlyR) with tdTomato (D1-MSN marker), confirming Cre-dependent expression. The methodology is well-documented with appropriate citations and viral construct details.

result: In vivo activation of PSAM4-GlyR with uPSEM792 increased c-fos expression in D1-MSNs expressing PSAM4-GlyR, indicating neuronal activation rather than inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C2, C12, C23, and C24 present converging evidence from immunohistochemistry showing increased c-fos in PSAM4-GlyR+ neurons (two-way ANOVA F1,34=30.55, p<0.0001) with no effect in non-transduced cells (C25). The use of c-fos as a marker is well-justified (C21, C22). The experimental design includes appropriate controls and statistical analysis with n=8-12 animals per group.

result: PSAM4-GlyR activation induced inward currents and depolarized D1-MSNs in whole-cell voltage-clamp and current-clamp recordings in a concentration-dependent manner.
evaluation: Claims C14, C15, C28-C30, and C33-C37 provide detailed electrophysiological measurements showing dose-dependent inward currents (10 nM: -43.0±10.1 pA; 50 nM: -275.5±57.1 pA) and membrane depolarization (10 nM: 6.4±2.0 mV; 50 nM: 20.9±3.4 mV). Control experiments (C27) demonstrate specificity. Statistical analyses are appropriate with paired t-tests and two-way ANOVA (F1,37=9.70, p=0.004).

result: PSAM4-GlyR activation decreased membrane resistance of D1-MSNs by approximately 30% at 50 nM uPSEM792.
evaluation: Claims C13, C31, and C32 document baseline membrane resistance (78.6±5.5 MΩ) consistent with prior literature (C31) and a significant 29.6±5.3% decrease with 50 nM uPSEM792 (p<0.0001, n=18). The methodology for measuring membrane resistance is clearly described with voltage steps.

result: The majority of D1-MSNs maintained action potential firing during PSAM4-GlyR activation, with only a subset entering depolarization block at higher agonist concentrations.
evaluation: Claims C17, C38-C40 provide quantitative data: all neurons (14/14) continued firing at 10 nM, while 10/16 continued firing and 6/16 entered depolarization block at 50 nM. Claim C41 identifies that neurons entering depolarization block had higher membrane resistance (92.4±5.2 vs 65.8±6.7 mΩ). Claims C70 and C86 correctly conclude that the ~30% decrease in membrane resistance was insufficient to prevent firing.

result: Cell-attached recordings demonstrated that PSAM4-GlyR activation induced action potential firing in D1-MSNs when neurons were depolarized to subthreshold potentials.
evaluation: Claims C18, C44, and C64 are supported by cell-attached recordings showing PSAM4-GlyR-induced firing at subthreshold depolarization (elevated K+), with appropriate controls (C45). Statistical analysis (C46: mixed-effects two-way ANOVA, F2,13=12.40, p=0.001) confirms significant interaction. Claims C42-C43 show no suppression of high K+-induced firing. This approach avoids artifacts from intracellular chloride dialysis in whole-cell recordings.

result: Sustained PSAM4-GlyR activation caused a rightward shift in the reversal potential from -61.4 mV (transient) to -44.2 mV (steady-state), with the magnitude of shift correlating with PSAM4-GlyR conductance.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 document the reversal potential shift with appropriate statistical analysis (linear regression, paired t-test t=5.73, p<0.0001, n=21). Claim C52 shows positive correlation between conductance and shift magnitude (r=0.57, p=0.0008). Claims C49-C51 describe the U-shaped I-V relationship and tail current augmentation, supporting chloride accumulation. Calculated reversal potentials (C92-C93) provide theoretical context.

result: PSAM4-GlyR activation reduced GABAergic inhibition in D1-MSNs through apparent cross-desensitization, with GABAA receptor reversal potential shifting from -60.9 mV to -51.6 mV in neurons showing PSAM4-GlyR reversal potential shifts.
evaluation: Claims C55-C56 provide detailed measurements showing decreased GABAA current amplitude (-33.4±6.0 vs -7.8±1.3 pA, p=0.01) and rightward shift in GABAA reversal potential (test of equal intercepts F1,21=18.3, p=0.0003) in neurons with >5 mV PSAM4-GlyR shift (n=5). Claim C57 shows no change in neurons without PSAM4-GlyR shift (n=3), supporting specificity. The mechanism is consistent with chloride accumulation.

result: The mechanism underlying PSAM4-GlyR-mediated depolarization involves chloride influx overwhelming homeostatic mechanisms, similar to sustained activation of other chloride conductances.
evaluation: Claims C53 and C67 are well-supported by multiple citations documenting chloride accumulation with sustained activation of GABAA receptors, glycine receptors, and halorhodopsin. Claim C69 correctly distinguishes between brief endogenous neurotransmitter activation and sustained exogenous agonist application. The mechanistic interpretation is consistent with the observed reversal potential shifts.

result: PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs is predominantly depolarizing at physiological membrane potentials with limited capacity for hyperpolarization.
evaluation: Claims C62, C65, C66, and C85 synthesize the electrophysiological findings. At resting potential (-83 mV), PSAM4-GlyR passes inward current and depolarizes neurons (supported by C14-C15, C28-C30, C33-C37). The limited hyperpolarizing capacity is supported by the U-shaped I-V relationship (C49-C50) and transient nature of outward currents at depolarized potentials.

result: The shunting efficacy of PSAM4-GlyR in D1-MSNs is limited due to their low membrane resistance (~78 MΩ) relative to other neurons, and increasing expression would likely exacerbate depolarization rather than improve inhibition.
evaluation: Claim C71 appropriately compares results to Magnus et al. 2019 where PSAM4-GlyR suppressed firing in cortical neurons. Claim C72 correctly interprets the correlation data (C52) showing that higher conductance correlates with greater reversal potential shift. Claim C73 provides a mechanistic explanation based on the measured membrane resistance (C31) and comparison to other neuron types.

result: In vivo, PSAM4-GlyR activation is predicted to increase the probability and duration of spontaneous depolarizations in D1-MSNs based on their membrane potential dynamics in awake behaving animals.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 make predictions about in vivo effects based on ex vivo data and cited literature (C76: Mahon et al. 2006). While the reasoning is logical, these are inferences rather than direct measurements. Claim C75 acknowledges that in vivo conditions (higher temperature, more synaptic inputs) would likely reduce shunting efficacy further, but this remains speculative without direct in vivo electrophysiology.

result: The increased c-fos expression observed in vivo is attributed to both PSAM4-GlyR-induced depolarization and loss of GABAergic inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C79-C81 synthesize the in vivo c-fos data (C23-C24) with the mechanistic findings from electrophysiology (depolarization: C33-C37; loss of GABAergic inhibition: C55-C58). The interpretation is well-supported by the convergent evidence, though the relative contributions of each mechanism cannot be quantified from the presented data.

result: PSAM4-GlyR-induced depolarization may cause calcium influx through voltage-gated channels and NMDA receptors, potentially confounding experimental interpretation.
evaluation: Claims C82-C84 present reasonable speculation about potential calcium signaling consequences of depolarization, supported by appropriate citations about NMDA receptor properties and calcium signaling. However, these are explicitly speculative ("may allow," "it is possible") and no calcium measurements are presented. This represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than a demonstrated result.

result: PSAM4-GlyR may not be suitable for neuronal silencing in all cell types, highlighting the need for validation in specific cell types prior to behavioral studies.
evaluation: Claims C87-C89 present appropriate conclusions and recommendations based on the study's findings. The data clearly demonstrate that PSAM4-GlyR failed to inhibit D1-MSNs despite working in other cell types (C71). The recommendation for cell-type-specific validation (C88) is a reasonable and important practical implication of the findings.

result: PSAM4-GlyR is a chloride-permeable chemogenetic tool proposed for neuronal inhibition, with advantages over DREADDs in terms of specificity.
evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C11 accurately describe PSAM4-GlyR based on established literature (Magnus et al. 2019). Claims C7-C8 correctly cite limitations of DREADDs (Saloman et al. 2016; Gomez et al. 2017; Manvich et al. 2018). These claims provide appropriate background context for the study.

result: The internal recording solution contained 12.8 mM Cl⁻ to mimic the natural chloride reversal potential in MSNs (ECl ~ -62 mV).
evaluation: Claim C26 describes a critical methodological detail supported by appropriate citations (Misgeld et al. 1982; Bracci and Panzeri 2006). This is important for interpreting the electrophysiological results, as the internal chloride concentration determines the initial reversal potential.

result: Neuronal silencing with chloride conductances is challenging due to dependence on hyperpolarization and/or shunting, unlike excitatory chemogenetic tools which have been more successful.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 provide appropriate context about the challenges of inhibitory vs excitatory chemogenetics, supported by relevant citations (Gomez et al. 2017; Manvich et al. 2018; Wiegert et al. 2017; Doyon et al. 2016). Claim C68 correctly describes endogenous neurotransmitter dynamics. These claims establish the conceptual framework for understanding why PSAM4-GlyR failed in D1-MSNs.
